walkthroughs.body_html: Howard (2001): poor diet linked to lower concentration. Smith & Noble (1995): 'costs of free schooling' include uniform, trips, equipment. Gibson & Asthana (1999): low income correlates with low achievement. Ridge (2002): children in poverty know about cost early.

Douglas (1964): middle-class parents more involved. Bernstein (1971): working-class restricted code vs middle-class elaborated code aligns with school. Sugarman (1970): working-class values of fatalism, immediate gratification clash with school. Critics: blames the victim.

Bourdieu (1984): middle-class kids inherit cultural capital — knowledge, manners, accent, tastes that school rewards. Combined with economic capital (private tutors) and social capital (networks). Working-class kids face structural disadvantage, not deficient culture.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between material and cultural deprivation?
options: Material deprivation is about a lack of clothing; cultural deprivation is about not visiting museums.

Material deprivation refers to lack of physical/economic resources (housing, books, food); cultural deprivation refers to lack of skills, values and norms (e.g. parental attitudes to education) that are claimed to support achievement.
Material and cultural deprivation are two names for the same poverty.
Government funding for the arts.

mcqs.q: What are Weber's three dimensions of stratification?
options: Weber agreed with Marx that class is purely economic.
Material deprivation is about a lack of clothing; cultural deprivation is about not visiting museums.
Class (economic position in markets), status (social honour/prestige), and party (organised power) — Weber argued these can vary independently, unlike Marx's economic-determinism view.
Weber's three dimensions are upper, middle and working class.
